knownFor: Lycian bishop and martyr who argued against Origen that the same body rises, and who praised the life of chastity.
shortDescription: Methodius of Olympus was a bishop in Lycia, in the south of Asia Minor. He wrote the Banquet, in which ten young women praise the unmarried life given to God, and a dialogue against Origen arguing that the same body will rise.
datesNote: No old source gives a year for his birth or his death. Jerome says he was crowned with martyrdom at the end of the recent persecution or, as others affirm, under the emperors Decius and Valerian, who reigned before it. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing in his lifetime, asked how he dared to write against Origen now. A century shown for him comes from the modern dating of those emperors and of Jerome, not from the sources.
placeNote: Olympus, a city in Lycia, where he was bishop; Tyre, where Jerome says he was bishop afterwards; Chalcis in Greece, where Jerome says he was crowned with martyrdom

keyWorks.title: The Banquet of the Ten Virgins
keyWorks.about: A dialogue in which ten women praise chastity in a garden. One friend asks another to repeat the speeches given at a feast held by Virtue under a wide, shady tree. One speaker says the praise of virginity does not do away with marriage, and Virtue, the host, says chastity keeps the tongue, the eyes, the hands and the mind pure, not the body alone. It ends with a hymn to Christ, the Bridegroom.

keyWorks.title: On the Resurrection
keyWorks.about: Argues against Origen that the body is no fetter and rises again. A person is soul and body joined, and God dissolves the body in death and remakes it, as a craftsman melts down a spoiled statue and casts it again. Long passages survive in Greek in Epiphanius, and a later summary by Photius.

keyWorks.title: On Free Will
keyWorks.about: A treatise Jerome lists as his, also against Origen.

traces: Epiphanius of Salamis, writing against Origen later in the fourth century, chose to rest his case on what the blessed Methodius had said in On the Resurrection, and set it out word for word. He called him a learned man who fought hard for the truth.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus copied a passage from his sermon on the martyrs into a set of testimonies from earlier bishops on how God became man. In it Methodius says martyrdom is so precious that Christ himself honored it, to crown the manhood he had come down into.
Photius read On the Resurrection centuries later and summed it up, and his summary keeps what Methodius said of Origen's teaching on the body.
A later Syriac chronicle retells his story of Phidias, a sculptor who poured oil before his ivory statue so that it would last, from the work he addressed to Aglaophon on the resurrection.
Three fragments of his work against Porphyry are held, from a later collection, the Parallels of John of Damascus. John of Damascus, writing on the use of images in worship, cited him too.
remembered: Remembered as Origen's opponent. The church historian Socrates of Constantinople, who defended Origen, names him first among the four who reviled Origen.

Honored as a martyr. Jerome says he was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece, and Theodoret calls him the holy Methodius, bishop and martyr. Photius calls him Saint Methodius, Bishop and Martyr.
Jerome set him among the church's writers, praised the polished and logical style of his books against Porphyry, and called On the Resurrection an excellent work.
Theodoret named him with Ignatius, Irenaeus and Hippolytus among the bishops and martyrs whose words witness to the faith, and among the teachers of the church whose teaching he followed.

uncertain: His death. Jerome gives two times: at the end of the recent persecution, or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian, earlier emperors. An editor of Jerome notes that the words on Decius and Valerian are missing from the oldest manuscript, at Verona. Where he died rests on Jerome alone, and no held source tells how he died.
His sees. Jerome makes him bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre; Socrates names Olympus only. John of Damascus, writing much later, calls him bishop of Patara, also in Lycia.
His second name. Epiphanius calls him Methodius, also called Eubulius. Euboulios is also the friend who asks for the story in the Banquet; the sources do not say why he bore the name.

Socrates of Constantinople tells of his change of heart, and Socrates defended Origen. He names the dialogue in which Methodius of Olympus praised him: Xenon, a work the Library does not hold. Eusebius of Caesarea, as Jerome quotes him, asks how Methodius dared to write against Origen now. Jerome says Eusebius makes the same complaint against Methodius that Rufinus, Jerome's opponent, makes against Jerome himself, but Eusebius's words do not themselves say that Methodius praised Origen.

Eusebius's question. Jerome, who reports it, calls Eusebius an Arian, a follower of Arius, who taught that there was a time when the Son was not. Pamphilus of Caesarea had written a defense of Origen before Eusebius wrote his.

Origen's side. Origen's teaching on the body is told as Methodius gave it. The soul lived without a body before the fall, the first sin, and was given the body afterwards as a fetter. At the resurrection only each person's form rises, on another, spiritual body. Origen's own book On First Principles, held only in English from the Latin of Rufinus, a later translator, says it is the body that rises, our own, as a spiritual body. Rufinus says he left out or changed passages on the Trinity, and made unclear sentences plainer from Origen's other works.

The summary. What the dialogue On the Resurrection is about, and its account of Origen, come from the summary Photius made centuries later. Methodius's own Greek survives only in the long passages Epiphanius copied, and the Greek of the Banquet is not held.
Socrates's reason. He argues that the four who attacked Origen, each on one point, never charged him with unsound views on the Trinity, and so bear witness to his soundness.

Jerome also says he answered Porphyry, a philosopher of his own time who wrote books against the Christians and their Scriptures, in a work of ten thousand lines. Jerome names him again, with Eusebius and Apollinaris, among those who answered Porphyry's attack on the book of Daniel.

The Banquet's other speakers give more of its teaching. The first says the plant of virginity was sent down from heaven late, after the human race had moved by stages from marrying sisters, to one wife, to restraint, to virginity. Thekla, a guest in the book, is given the larger crown; the book does not say who she is. In a closing talk, a soul that feels desire and holds its course is called better, as the pilot who saves his ship in a storm is better than one who sails in a calm.

On the Resurrection has a second image beside the statue: sin is like a fig tree grown into the stones of a temple, torn out by the roots so that the temple can stand again. Methodius also quotes Justin of Neapolis, a man near the apostles in time, on the resurrection.

briefReferences: Methodius, The Banquet of the Ten Virgins, tr. William R. Clark: one friend asks another to repeat the speeches; the rough, steep path; Virtue, a tall woman in a robe white as snow, who embraces them like a mother; the ten guests and the wide, shady tree; her call to praise virginity; one guest's word that marriage is not abolished, and the moon and the stars; Virtue's word on the tongue, the eyes, the hands and the mind; the hymn under the tree to Christ, the Bridegroom.

Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 83, tr. Ernest Cushing Richardson: bishop of Olympus in Lycia; the Banquet and On the Resurrection, against Origen; crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece at the end of the recent persecution or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian.

Photius, Bibliotheca 234 (extract), tr. W. R. Clark: the dialogue's subject; Origen's teaching as Methodius gave it, the soul without a body before the fall, the body given afterwards as a fetter, and only the form rising, on another spiritual body; Cain, who committed murder in this body; a human being soul and body joined.

Methodius, On the Resurrection, tr. Clark, with the Greek Epiphanius copies, Panarion 64, ed. Karl Holl: those who turn bones and flesh into allegory so that the resurrection is without flesh; the craftsman who melts down a beautiful statue an envious man has spoiled and casts it again; God, seeing man, his fairest work, spoiled by envy, dissolving him and remaking him.
Jerome, Apology against Rufinus I.11, tr. W. H. Fremantle: Eusebius, in the sixth book of his defense of Origen, asks how Methodius could dare to write now against Origen.
Eusebius, Church History VI.39 and VII.11, tr. Arthur Cushman McGiffert: Decius follows Philip; a confessor of Valerian's time lived on until the persecution of Eusebius's own day.
Epiphanius, Panarion 64.12, Greek, ed. Karl Holl: he chose to rest on what the blessed Methodius had said in On the Resurrection against Origen, and set it out word for word.

Socrates, Church History VI.13, tr. A. C. Zenos, with the Greek ed. Robert Hussey and as Hans Lietzmann reprints it: first of four who reviled Origen; worthless men who seek notice by decrying those who excel them; after railing against Origen, as if retracting, he praised him in a dialogue he called Xenon.

quotationOriginals.modern: The moon may be greater than the stars, but its light does not put out the light of the other stars.
quotationOriginals.printed: although the moon may be greater than the stars, the light of the other stars is not destroyed by the moonlight.
quotationOriginals.work: Methodius, The Banquet of the Ten Virgins, Discourse II.1, Theophila's speech, tr. William R. Clark, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek of the Banquet is not held, so the modern English follows Clark's English alone. The chapter heading gives the plain sense: Marriage Not Abolished by the Commendation of Virginity (lines 30269-30270).

quotationOriginals.modern: For the statue cannot be lost while it is in the same craftsman's hands, even if it is melted down into its material again. It can be restored. But the blemishes and the damage can be lost, for they melt away. They cannot be restored.
quotationOriginals.printed: For it is impossible for an image under the hands of the original artist to be lost, even if it be melted down again, for it may be restored; but it is possible for blemishes and injuries to be put off, for they melt away and cannot be restored
quotationOriginals.work: Methodius, On the Resurrection I, as Epiphanius copies it, Panarion 64.34, ed. Karl Holl; English tr. William R. Clark, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6
quotationOriginals.original: τῷ μὲν γὰρ ἀγάλματι ἀπολέσϑαι οὖκ ἔστιν ὑπὸ τῷ αὐτῷ τεχνίτῃ ὄντι, χἂν πάλιν eis ὕλην λυϑῇ, ἀποχατασταϑῆναι δὲ ἔστι" τοῖς δὲ αἴσχεσι χαὶ λωβήμασιν ἀπολέσϑαι μὲν ἔστιν (τήχονται γάρ), ἀποχατασταϑ'ῆναι δὲ οὐκ ἔστι
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is printed as the damaged scan reads it; it reads κἂν πάλιν εἰς ὕλην λυθῇ and ἀποκατασταθῆναι, and Oehler's print of the same passage confirms the reading (epiphanius_panarion-haer-48-69, lines 22929-22933). Holl's notes record that two manuscripts lack ὄντι and one reads χυθῇ, which leaves the sense unchanged (lines 35747-35750). The modern English follows the Greek: statue for ἄγαλμα, where Clark prints image, and material for ὕλη, since the statue is of gold or other material (Clark, lines 35424-35425); the same craftsman for τῷ αὐτῷ τεχνίτῃ, where Clark prints the original artist.

quotationOriginals.modern: Worthless people, who cannot be noticed on their own, want to be seen by finding fault with their betters. Methodius was the first to fall into this.
quotationOriginals.printed: Worthless characters, and such as are destitute of ability to attain eminence themselves, often seek to get into notice by decrying those who excel them. And first Methodius, bishop of a city in Lycia named Olympus, labored under this malady
quotationOriginals.work: Socrates of Constantinople, Church History VI.13, tr. A. C. Zenos, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 2; Greek as Hans Lietzmann prints it, and ed. Robert Hussey
quotationOriginals.original: οἱ εὐτελεῖς καὶ dp’ ἑαυτῶν μὴ δυνάμενοι φαίνεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ ψέγειν τοὺς ἑαυτῶν κρείττονας δείκνυσθαι βούλονται. τοῦτο πέπονθε πρῶτος Μεθόδιος
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is printed as the scan reads it; for dp’ it reads ἀφ᾽, as Hussey's print of Socrates has it (socrates_historia-ecclesiastica-tomus2, line 12878), which is damaged further on. The modern English follows the Greek: wish to be seen for δείκνυσθαι βούλονται, and the first to fall into this for τοῦτο πέπονθε πρῶτος, where Zenos prints often seek to get into notice and first labored under this malady.
